text: Mercury. The silver liquid in old thermometers. In October twenty twenty six, a startup said it had turned it into real gold. Alchemists tried this for nearly two thousand years. Some turned out to be tricksters. So is this the real thing? <#0.3#> Gold is rare, and it never rusts. That's why families keep it for generations. All of it ever mined would fit in one cube, twenty two metres across. For centuries, people tried to make it. Even Isaac Newton. <#0.2#> Chemistry can't turn one metal into another. <#0.2#> Physics can. In nineteen nineteen, Ernest Rutherford broke into the atom. In nineteen forty one, Harvard scientists hit mercury with neutrons, and got a few atoms of radioactive gold. In twenty twenty five, the Large Hadron Collider team showed it makes specks of gold from lead, gone in a split second. <#0.3#> The secret? Every element is a number: the protons in the centre of its atoms. Gold is seventy nine. Mercury is eighty. Next-door neighbours. <#0.2#> Fusion fires fast neutrons into mercury. Each hit knocks a neutron out, and the atom turns unstable. Within days, a proton turns into a neutron. Eighty becomes seventy nine. Mercury becomes gold. <#0.3#> The catch: some of the fresh gold is radioactive. The company's own paper says it must wait almost eighteen years to be less radioactive than a banana. Gold made today would pass that test around twenty forty four. <#0.3#> Marathon says it beat CERN's gold record by ten times. Alchemists faced one test: show us the gold. Marathon hasn't shown how much, and no one else has checked yet. A big fusion plant might make a few tonnes a year. And no fusion plant sells power yet. <#0.3#> Newton tried with a furnace. Now, someone says fusion did it. Imagine two gold rings, identical atom for atom. One mined, one made. Which would you give to someone you love?
